stories.title: Guwahati: Fight against flood hits roadblock of unplanned growth, drainage gaps
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: GUWAHATI: Guwahati’s recurring urban flooding has exposed gaps in the city’s drainage planning, with rapid construction, expanding transport infrastructure and overlapping departmental responsibilities complicating efforts to build a flood-resilient urban system.

The Assam Government has asked consultants to revise the proposed Comprehensive Drainage Master Plan for Guwahati and the Detailed Project Report for the Bahini-Bharalu Basin to identify shortcomings and strengthen measures against chronic waterlogging.

Reports in Dispur said the problem extended beyond the capacity of individual drains, as the city’s rapid expansion through flyovers, roads, residential complexes and commercial projects had altered natural water-flow patterns in several areas.
Guwahati has 24 flyovers and bridges either operational or forming part of its expanding transport network.
While these projects have improved connectivity, questions remain over whether adequate storm-water drainage provisions were incorporated into their planning.

The city’s location along the Brahmaputra and its network of natural channels and tributaries has historically allowed wetlands, low-lying areas and drainage channels to absorb and carry excess rainwater.
Rapid urbanisation and encroachment, however, have placed increasing pressure on these systems.

A senior PWD official also pointed to overlapping responsibilities among agencies, including the Public Works Department, Guwahati Municipal Corporation and other urban bodies, in constructing and maintaining roads and drains.
Changes in desiltation responsibilities have also contributed to uncertainty over the agency responsible for specific stretches.
“There has to be a construction plan and maintenance plan, which is missing in Guwahati,” the official said.
Urban planners and civic experts have called for an integrated drainage map with clearly defined drainage hierarchies, maintenance responsibilities and standard operating procedures.

They have also stressed coordination among the GMC, PWD, GMDA and other agencies, along with separation of storm-water and sewage networks, protection of wetlands and natural channels, action against encroachment and mandatory drainage provisions in major infrastructure projects.

article_sentences: GUWAHATI: The Assam Panchayat & Rural Development (P&RD) Department has issued a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for assessment, prioritisation and mitigation of post-flood damages in Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat and Golaghat, which were severely affected by the floods in July 2026.

The SOP lays down a time-bound mechanism for assessing damage to rural roads, drainage systems, water bodies, embankments, public buildings, houses, sanitation infrastructure, agricultural land and livelihood assets.

The restoration programme will be carried out by combining resources from VB-G RAM G, PMAY-G, the 15th Finance Commission Grants, the Assam State Rural Livelihoods Mission (ASRLMS), the National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS), and other government programmes.
The SOP provides for assessment at the gaon panchayat (GP), block and district levels.
At the GP level, officials and elected representatives will conduct field assessments, identify damaged assets and affected households, capture geo-tagged photographs and prepare priority lists.
The block-level committee will technically scrutinise and consolidate GP reports, prepare programme-wise action plans and ensure that proposed works comply with scheme guidelines.
At the district level, the District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA) under ASDMA will review and prioritise proposals, facilitate inter-departmental convergence and monitor implementation.

A major focus of the SOP is providing immediate wage employment to flood-affected people through permissible works under VB-G RAM G. Priority works include restoration of rural roads, culverts, cross-drainage structures, canals, traditional water bodies, flood diversion drains, embankments, community buildings and other public assets damaged by floods.
The SOP also permits livelihood-orientated individual beneficiary schemes, subject to applicable approvals.
These include cattle, goat, piggery and poultry shelters, farm ponds, vermicompost structures and plantation-related activities.

For future flood preparedness, the government has identified construction of flood relief shelters, flood diversion channels, drainage systems, embankments, flood protection walls and storm-water drains as priority interventions wherever permissible.

The SOP specifies that restoration of the same asset under VB-G RAM G should ordinarily be permitted only once and requires a no-objection certificate from the line department concerned for the restoration of assets belonging to other departments.

stories.headline: Let’s save Kashmir’s geological treasures from vandalisation!
stories.title: Let’s save Kashmir’s geological treasures from vandalisation!
stories.summary: Can you imagine how fast we are losing Karewas, which are geological and archeological repositories, being vandalised for earth excavation? 18 metric tons of clay, sand and bajri have been illegally excavated in Karewas of Budgam and Pulwama district in the last 5 years alone. The damage is far more than earth excavation. We need to understand that Karewas are not just raised mounds of earth. These Karewas were formed due to tectonic events which occured at different intervals during the uplift of the Pir Panjal Range due to Himalayan orogeny. Considered to be an important part of Kashmir’s eco-system. Karewas known as Wuder are a flat-topped tableland and consist of conglomerate, silt, clay, sands and lignite beds. What is important is that the climatic and tectonic record during the last 1.6 million years is well preserved in the sediments of Karewas of Kashmir valley. Years ago, fossils of Elephant species called Elephas hysudricus were found in Karewas of Pulwama and Budgam areas. Fossils of Sivatherium giganteum, an extinct species of Giraffe, have also been found in Samboora karewas near Pampore. Besides fish scales were found in Karewas of Gogjee Pathri and upper mountain areas of Liddermud and Yusmarg in Budgam district. Instead of taking measures to preserve these geological treasures, successive regimes have failed to stop earth mining in Karewas. Many karewas have been flattened by organised earth mafia using machines in Budgam and Pulwama districts. It is more concerning that excavated soil from these karewas has been mostly used in so-called developmental projects including construction of new roads in Kashmir and Railway projects. Wanton excavation of Karewas has led to soil erosion and extensive siltation of waterways and water bodies in Kashmir. Karewas help to retain rain water preventing flash floods and sudden rise in water levels in water bodies in its downstream areas. The massive destruction of Karewas prompted a noted environmental activist Dr Raja Muzaffar Bhat to approach the National Green Tribunal (NGT) stating that illegal clay, sand and bajri mining at Zadoora, Rangeen Kultreh villages of Pulwama and Chadoora Budgam had destroyed around 1000 kanals of land. This has led to immense loss to local apple, plum and almond orchards. The NGT constituted Joint Committee had in April this year visited the sites to ascertain the extent of illegal mining and the quantity of the clay and bajri which has been illegally extracted. The report of the Joint Committee comprising senior officers from Ministry of Environment Forest & Climate Change -MoEF, Central Pollution Control Board –CPCB, J&K Pollution Control Committee, Deputy Commissioners of Budgam and Pulwama has confirmed large scale illegal earth mining in karewas of Pulwama and Budgam in last 5 years. The report reveals that more than 18 lakh metric tons of clay ,sand , gravel has been illegally excavated in Zadoora , Gowherpora and Rangeen Kultreh villages of Pulwama and Budgam districts. Out of 18 lakh MTs , 130500 MTs of material has been excavated from Gowherpora and rangeen Kultreh villages of Chadoora Budgam and around 5 lakhs MTs from Zadoora village of Pulwama in Hastikhud area. The report quoting Mining Department J&K Government mentions that illegal excavation work took place due to law and order situation post article 370 abrogation and COVID 19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021. The report mentions that a company undertook earth mining at Gowherpora without any Environmental Clearance. A report filed by Ecology, Environment and Remote Sensing also confirms large scale mining has taken place as per satellite imagery between 2014 to 2026. The petitioner Dr Raja Muzaffar has sought a probe by CBI and ACB against the officials who allowed plunder of Karewas. stories.headline: NSA Doval to visit China today to attend Special Representatives talks with FM Wang
stories.title: NSA Doval to visit China today to attend Special Representatives talks with FM Wang
stories.summary: National Security Advisor Ajit Doval is scheduled to arrive in Beijing on Monday to take part in the India-China Special Representatives (SR) talks on the boundary issue with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi. Doval and Wang are scheduled to hold the 25th round of SR talks on Tuesday, according to official sources. Both Doval and Wang are the designated SRs for the boundary talks mechanism, which was established in 2003 to comprehensively address the vexed boundary dispute of the India-China border spanning 3,488 km. While success eluded it in resolving the boundary dispute, officials on both sides regard the structured mechanism as a useful tool in addressing the recurring tensions between the two countries on various fronts. The upcoming talks assume significance as they are being held ahead of the much-anticipated visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to India to attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12-13. While there is no official confirmation about Xi’s visit, officials on both sides are optimistic about the Chinese leader’s participation, which could provide an opportunity for a meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the summit to discuss initiatives to take forward bilateral ties. The two leaders met in August last year on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin. Ahead of Doval-Wang talks in Beijing, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Saturday reiterated that peace and tranquillity along the border areas are prerequisite for good relations with China. His comments came amid reports of aggressive posturing by Chinese troops in Arunachal Pradesh's Upper Subansiri region in recent weeks. "I think we went through a particularly bad patch between the summer of 2020 and the autumn of 2024, and that was primarily an outcome of the situation in the border areas," Jaishankar said at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum in New Delhi on Saturday. "At the end of the day, peace and tranquillity in the border areas is a prerequisite for good relations, and the state of the border, to a very large measure, naturally would determine the state of the relations," he said. On the reports of stepped-up Chinese military activity near the Arunachal Pradesh border, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on August 12 that the China-India border situation is "generally stable at the moment”. China and India held the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on China-India Border Affairs, Guo said. “The two sides agreed to maintain communication via diplomatic and military channels and jointly uphold peace and tranquility in the border areas”, he said. External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal on August 11 said that India considers matters relating to border areas with China as "most serious" and asserted that maintaining peace and tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) is of "utmost importance", as the state of the frontier will govern the overall trajectory of bilateral ties. Earlier, New Delhi also trashed Beijing's criticism of its decision to formally identify 27 places and geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh by their standard names, emphasising that the state is an "inalienable and integral" part of India and nothing can change this "indisputable reality". China, which claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of South Tibet, has been releasing its set of names for the region since 2017. India termed the Chinese move as "vain and preposterous", asserting that such actions will not alter the "undeniable" reality that the state "was, is, and will" always remain an integral part of India.

stories.headline: EPG honours environmental champions, questions loss of open public spaces
stories.title: EPG honours environmental champions, questions loss of open public spaces
stories.summary: The Environmental Policy Group (EPG) on Saturday commemorated its departed co-founders and remembered its mentor and ideologue, late Syed Nassarullah Shah, on his fourth death anniversary at a function held at the Institution of Engineers, Srinagar. The annual function brought together members of civil society, academicians, lawyers, environmental activists and researchers to remember the contributions of those associated with the environmental movement and to recognise individuals who have made significant contributions towards environmental conservation and public causes. A seminar on the theme “Loss of Green/Open Spaces and Its Impact on Environment” was also held as part of the programme. Former Chairman of the Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission and former Commissioner-Secretary, General Administration Department, Farooq Ahmad Lone was the chief guest. A major highlight of the function was the recognition of environmental activist Abdul Hamid Bhat, CEO of Rahim Greens, for having planted a recorded 3.5 lakh saplings and plants. Bhat has set himself the ambitious target of planting one million trees. The EPG acknowledged Bhat’s contribution in the field of plantation and environmental conservation, particularly in view of the personal challenges he has faced. Bhat had suffered a serious accident after being hit by a truck while cycling on the Bypass around a year ago. He has since recovered to the extent of being able to walk with the support of a stick and a helper, while continuing his commitment to environmental conservation. In his welcome address, the EPG Convenor, Faiz Bakshi lauded environmental activists for continuing their conservation efforts despite difficult circumstances and expressed serious concern over the rapid disappearance of green and open spaces. He particularly referred to the proposed construction-related plans concerning the Polo Ground, describing the open space as a lifeline for thousands of youngsters who use it for sports, recreation and indoor games throughout the year. He cautioned that the loss of such spaces could deprive young people of healthy recreational outlets and make them more vulnerable to drug addiction and other social problems. Bakshi said the EPG had made several representations to the Government, from the Chief Minister to officials at lower levels of administration, but had not received a response. He added that efforts to obtain complete information through the Right to Information mechanism had also failed to provide clarity, leaving important details about the proposed interventions shrouded in secrecy. Referring to the chief guest's contribution as Deputy Commissioner, Srinagar, the Convenor recalled Farooq Ahmad Lone's role in allotting 32 kanals of land at Khonmoh for the Permian-Triassic Park.. He said the administrative decision had helped preserve fossils and a geological section associated with a significant global event in Earth's history. “If that decision had not been taken, the fossils and the section, which are a repository of a significant global event of the Great Dying, could have ended up being destroyed through stone mining, crushed aggregate and cement-related activity,” he said, saluting Lone for what he described as an administrative and historic act. Chairman of the EPG Legal Committee, Advocate Shafqat Nazir, dealt at length with the consequences of losing green and open spaces, particularly for young people. He argued that there should be more open spaces, playgrounds and sports infrastructure to provide young people with constructive alternatives to drugs. He pointed out what he described as a contradiction between policy declarations against drug addiction and the disappearance of spaces that provide opportunities for sports and recreation. Advocate Nazir said that if the Polo Ground gives way to a flyover, football, hockey and rugby grounds as well as the Sunday market would disappear. Referring to constitutional provisions and Supreme Court judgments, he spoke about the Government's obligation to protect public spaces, the environment and public health. He referred to the doctrine of public trust recognised in Supreme Court judgments, including those associated with V.S. Mutappa and M.C. Mehta, arguing that public resources such as land, water, forests and open spaces are held by the Government as a trustee for the public rather than as an absolute owner. He questioned whether stakeholders, including youngsters, Polo View shopkeepers and the Pollution Control Committee, had been consulted about the proposed project and, if so, why their feedback had not been made public. “The amount spent on the flyover will not buy us even ‘one Chinar’,” he concluded. Former Chief Town Planner Iftikhar Hakim, in his presentation, spoke about the loss of open and green spaces, wetlands and water bodies in Srinagar over the past several decades. He warned that allowing further construction on open spaces identified for protection under the Master Plan-2035 would undermine Srinagar's heritage character. Hakim also referred to the earth-filling of the Nowgam Flood Absorption Basin for setting up an industrial and warehousing area, despite restrictions on development and construction in the area under the Master Plan. He warned that continuing with such interventions could increase the city's vulnerability to flooding. Prof. Javed Hussain Mir of the Islamic University of Science and Technology spoke about the challenges facing the environment, natural resources and the livelihoods of citizens. Referring to various surveys and research findings, he highlighted the positive impact of green environments and plants on human well-being and stressed the importance of nature-based solutions for conservation of natural resources and improving human well-being. Chairman of the RTI Movement and Climate Action Group, Dr Raja Muzaffar Bhat, recalled his long association with late Syed Nassarullah Shah and paid tribute to his oratorical and drafting skills, crusading spirit and commitment to public causes. He described Shah as a fearless campaigner who was prepared to take on powerful interests in pursuit of people's and societal causes. He recalled his contribution to the human rights and Right to Information movements and said the best tribute to his memory would be to carry forward his legacy. Ajaz Rasool said that his association with Syed Nassarullah dated back to drafting the EPG flood-related PIL way back in 2015. He was very much impressed by his vocabulary and drafting skills. He added that environmental activists need to be more proactive if their efforts to conserve natural resources; otherwise, our future generations will curse us. Chief guest Farooq Ahmad Lone commended the EPG for organising the annual event in memory of Syed Nassarullah Shah, late Syed Abdul Rashid Shah and late Mohammad Ramzan Khan (Gurezi), who had co-founded the Environmental Policy Group and contributed to its activities. He said the well-being of the environment was intrinsically linked to the well-being of society and observed that the presentations made during the function were particularly relevant in the context of climate change and global warming. Lone congratulated the awardees and described them as crusaders for environmental protection. He was felicitated with a Chinar, the emblem of Kashmir, carved out of walnut wood. The EPG also honoured late Syed Abdul Rashid Shah, Co-founder and Trustee of EPG, posthumously, with the award being received by his family members. Late G.H. Kango, former PCCF Forests and Chairman PEC, was also honoured posthumously, with family members receiving the recognition. Other awardees and recipients of mementoes included Er. Iftikhar Hakim, Prof. Javed Hussain Mir, Syed Sammi Nassarullah Shah, Advocates Shafqat Nazir and Shabir A. Bhat of the EPG Legal Team, Dr Raja Muzaffar Bhat, Er. Ajaz Rasool, Dr G.N. Qasba, Gowhar Maqbool, Advocate Rasikh Rasool, Ajaz Ahmad Dar, Rauf Tramboo, Shahala Sheikh and Faiz Bakshi. In his vote of thanks, EPG Co-Convenor Dr M.M. Shuja thanked the chief guest and participants for attending the programme. Remembering Syed Nassarullah Shah as a powerful voice for society, human rights, the RTI movement, environmental protection and social causes, Dr Shuja said he had also been a champion of public interest litigation and had drafted more than two dozen PILs. He recalled the last words spoken to him by Shah around two hours before his death: “Follow the PILs and petitions — strengthen the organisation — continue service to society.” The programme was anchored by EPG Co-founder and Trustee Peerzada Fayaz Ahmad, while the award ceremony was conducted by Dr Tauseef Bhat, EPG Co-founder and Trustee, who also recalled his long association with Syed Nassarullah Shah and Syed Abdul Rashid Shah.

stories.headline: NC made promises it could never fulfil: Akhoon
stories.title: NC made promises it could never fulfil: Akhoon
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 23: Jammu and Kashmir Apni Party State Vice President Mohammad Syed Akhoon on Sunday launched a sharp attack on the ruling National Conference (NC), alleging that the party has “reduced itself to a power-hungry organisation” and accusing it of misleading people with promises he claimed were unrealistic and difficult to fulfil. Addressing a public gathering at Brein-Nishat in Srinagar, chaired by Apni Party president Syed Mohammad Altaf Bukhari, Akhoon said his decision to leave the NC after decades of association had surprised many people. Taking aim at his former party, Akhoon alleged that the NC had become more focused on retaining power than addressing the dignity, aspirations and day-to-day concerns of the people. Recalling his association with the NC, Akhoon said he had openly opposed what he described as “unrealistic” promises made in the party’s election manifesto. He claimed that he had raised his concerns during a working committee meeting attended by senior leaders, including Dr Farooq Abdullah and Omar Abdullah. Akhoon said he had specifically questioned the feasibility of promises relating to enhanced ration, 12 LPG cylinders, 200 units of free electricity and one lakh jobs. “I told them we should not make promises that cannot be fulfilled. We should not mislead people,” he said, claiming that he subsequently faced action after expressing similar views publicly. Akhoon said he had remained associated with the National Conference since 1967 and had worked alongside several senior leaders during his long political career. He said he eventually decided to leave the party after concluding that it had drifted away from the principles with which he had been associated. He also criticised the state of civic infrastructure in Srinagar, alleging that residents in the city’s core areas continue to face inadequate basic amenities. Akhoon claimed that some remote and mountainous areas have better civic facilities than several localities in the heart of Srinagar. Explaining his decision to join the Apni Party, Akhoon said he had spent nearly two years assessing the political situation before taking the decision. “I spent nearly two years assessing the political situation before taking the step. I found Altaf Bukhari to be an honest leader committed to addressing unemployment and the everyday concerns of the people,” he said. Akhoon also defended Bukhari against allegations levelled against him by political opponents, describing the Apni Party president as a self-made individual with an established family background and rejecting claims that he required support from any outside agency. Referring to the recent increase in electricity tariffs, Akhoon accused the NC government of failing to honour its promise of providing 200 units of free electricity. He said the tariff increase had instead added to the financial burden on economically weaker sections. Akhoon also criticised what he described as the NC’s internal approach to political representation. Referring to the Independence Day function, he alleged that elected legislators were overlooked while prominence was given to a defeated candidate, which he said reflected the party’s priorities. He further alleged that several individuals currently holding important positions in the NC belonged to families that had “backstabbed” Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah in the past and contributed to his imprisonment. Appealing to people to strengthen the Apni Party, Akhoon urged voters to support Altaf Bukhari’s leadership for addressing unemployment and other public issues. He also claimed that people attending the rally had gathered voluntarily and without monetary inducements, contrasting it with what he alleged was the practice of some political parties of mobilising crowds through financial incentives.

Indian debt markets are shut on Wednesday for a local holiday.

Iran has denounced the planned US measures, while calling out for a diplomatic resolution.
